triage.rationale: The description fully specifies the function signature, file location, detection order (worktree-local bin/ then PATH), and its consumers, leaving no material design decision open.

payload.title: Add a user-level template directory so overrides are not per-project only
payload.description: templatecmd resolves a template as <project_root>/.endless/templates/<name>.local.tmpl, then <name>.tmpl, then the Go embed. That is per-project only: a user who wants the same handoff or guide wording across every project they work on must copy the override into each one, and re-copy it whenever a project is added. Add a user-level layer (e.g. ~/.config/endless/templates/) between the project layer and the embed, so precedence runs project .local -> project committed -> user -> embedded. Surfaced from E-2030, where gating the guide on report_gate raised the question of where a user edits shipped text.

triage.rationale: The description pins down the exact resolution order, the new precedence slot, and a concrete path shape (~/.config/endless/templates/), leaving only mechanical implementation.

payload.title: Re-arm verify scripts that drive the endless-go hook from a bare shell
payload.description: E-1962 made `hook claude` a silent no-op on an unrecognized agent harness, and a bare shell is one. Verify scripts that impersonate a session by piping into `endless-go hook claude` stopped exercising anything when it landed, without failing: half of what they assert is that the hook stays silent, and that passes against a dead hook. Confirmed in tests/tasks/e-1953-verify.sh.
payload.analysis:
# The failure is silent, which is why it survived a landing

`hook claude` returns immediately on an unrecognized agent harness (E-1962):
exit 0, no stdout, no side effects. A bare shell is unrecognized.

Any verify script that impersonates a session by piping a payload into
`endless-go hook claude` therefore stopped exercising anything the moment
E-1962 landed. Nothing announced it, because roughly half of what such a
script asserts is that the hook stays SILENT — a turn allowed to end, a
gate-off project, a subagent's return value, a `$FULL` license. Every one of
those passes against a hook that does nothing at all.

So the suite does not fail. It hollows out, and keeps reporting green.

## Confirmed instance

`tests/tasks/e-1953-verify.sh` pipes into `go_sandbox hook claude` at three
call sites and never exports `CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT`. It passes from inside a
Claude session, which exports that variable to its subprocesses, and is hollow
from a plain terminal — which is where a pre-land gate is actually run.

## How it was found

`tests/tasks/e-1975-verify.sh` had the identical bug. 106/106 from inside a
session; 89 passed / 16 failed from a bare shell. Every failure was an
assertion that needed the hook to DO something; every assertion expecting
silence passed. That asymmetry is the signature.

E-1975 fixed its own script two ways, both of which apply here:

  * every hook invocation goes through a helper that sets
    `CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT=cli`;
  * a preflight fires one payload that MUST produce a block and fails loudly if
    it does not, so a dead hook fails at the top rather than hollowing out the
    body.

## What to decide, not just what to fix

Fixing E-1953's script is mechanical. The open question is whether driving the
hook belongs in a shared helper rather than being re-derived per script. The
failure mode is silent and the precondition is invisible in the script itself,
so the next author will reproduce it — as this one did, in a script written
specifically to be careful about it.

triage.rationale: it names the symptom (verify scripts silently stopped exercising the hook) but not how to re-arm them—e.g. spoofing a recognized agent harness identity vs. changing the hook's no-op behavior for bare shells—which is a material design choice left unstated.

fields.description: Replaces apply-on-connect in monitor.DB(). A connect compares the DB's migration version against the binary's and acts BY DIRECTION. DB BEHIND the binary: the binary needs DDL that is absent, so an INSTALLED binary auto-applies forward -- unconditional in non-self_dev, which has one binary -- while a CANDIDATE binary refuses, because it may never migrate the real ledger, which is the 2026-08-10 failure exactly. DB AHEAD of the binary: HALT, for any binary. Per ED-1570 a binary works with exactly one schema version, so there is no compatibility window to evaluate; the binary must be upgraded, and rollback is served by restoring a pre-upgrade backup (E-1942). Accepted consequence: a self_dev branch carrying an unlanded migration has its candidate hook degraded for the whole pre-land window, which reduces what E-998 exercises on precisely those branches. That is the price of never letting unlanded code mutate the production schema, and it is worth paying.

payload.reason: Superseded by the ED-1566/1567/1570 cluster and by E-1972 -- not decided against: it was correct for May 2026. Both consumers it names are gone: E-1039 is obsolete (replaced by E-1704), and E-995's 'sandbox run' consumer is itself under review for deletion as YAGNI (E-1963). Its policy is reversed too -- 'detect worktree-local bin/, fall back to PATH' PREFERS the worktree binary, while ED-1570 requires exact schema-version agreement and E-1972 inverts the preference outright: always invoke main's known-good binary, delegating to a worktree's only when verified compatible (measured 2026-08-13: 89 of 135 worktrees pinned to their own binary, all 103 worktree binaries older than main's, one of which took session tracking down machine-wide). Finally E-1704's self-re-exec moves binary choice INTO the binary, so the shared call-site helper this decision specifies solves a problem that ceases to exist. Recorded as rejected only because 'superseded' is not expressible yet (E-1920); reclassify when it is.

payload.title: Replace apply-on-connect with versioned migrations and connect-time verification
payload.description: Umbrella for the schema-governance work E-1944 decided (ED-1566/1567/1570) after the 2026-08-10 outage, in which a candidate binary wrote a column the real ledger lacked and session tracking went down for 30 minutes. Adopt pressly/goose as the source of schema, demote schema.sql to a generated documentation artifact, stop monitor.DB() applying schema on every connect, and require exact binary/database version agreement — a DB behind an installed binary auto-applies forward, a DB ahead of any binary halts. Children were filed as free-floating siblings held together only by cleans_up E-1944; this gives them a home.

triage.rationale: The description names the concrete adopted approach (goose as schema source, schema.sql demoted to generated doc, removal of apply-on-connect, exact version-agreement semantics for behind/ahead cases), leaving only child tasks to implement each stated piece.

fields.description: ED-1570 halts a binary whose schema version is behind the database. After an upgrade migrates the ledger, every long-running process still holding the old binary image — background agents, the jobs runner — halts on its next connect and dies mid-flight, which can take down tens of live sessions at once. Halting is correct and must not be relaxed, so the fix is on the other side: detect processes running a superseded binary and restart them onto the new one as part of the upgrade, rather than letting them discover the mismatch one by one. E-1704 is the surface that decides which binary a process should be running; it moves that choice into the binary itself via self-re-exec, governed by E-1972's verified-compatible policy.

payload.outcome: Filed on a false premise. A verify script is a pre-land gate, valid only immediately before its own land, in its own worktree. A landed one is spent — nothing should run it again — so tests/tasks/e-1953-verify.sh being hollow against E-1962's harness gate costs nothing and is not a defect. Project-wide regression is 'go build/vet/test ./...' plus 'just test'. The real lesson belongs to the script being written, not to the ones already landed: E-1975's own gate had the same flaw and had to be fixed because it is about to run.

payload.title: Agent-invoked session machinery resolves the real ledger by default; only human-typed commands must name the database
payload.description: Carve-out from ED-1561, which requires an agent to name --db on every command reaching a database in a self_dev project. That is right for commands an agent CHOOSES to run against the ledger, and wrong for machinery it runs mechanically every turn under a contract, because there the correct database is not the caller's judgement -- it is fixed by whatever reads the result. Such a surface pins main when given no --db, as hook/channel/tmux already do; an explicit --db still wins. The test for membership is not 'does an agent type it' but 'does something else already fix which database is correct'.

payload.title: The minimizer's invariants outrank its deduplication objective: prose is deduplicated, actionable content never is
payload.description: ED-1557 makes deduplication against what the user already has half the minimizer's job. It contradicts the invariants the moment prior replies enter the fetched context: a verify command sent two turns ago is redundant by that objective and mandatory by invariant 3, and nothing said which wins. Measured on the fixture with a populated reply history, the table, code block and command were dropped TOGETHER in 2 of 8 live runs, leaving one sentence; with precedence stated, 0 of 8. The user is reading this message, not scrolling back to reassemble it. This binds any presentation too -- a preview that truncates mid-fence breaks the same rule in the reply itself.

fields.title: The minimizer deduplicates against artifacts the user must review anyway, not against what was already said in chat
fields.description: The objective is not "cut what was already said". It is: cut what the user will have to review ANYWAY -- what session status already shows, and what is written into a task, a decision or another durable artifact. Saying it in chat too means they read it twice. An earlier chat reply is not such an artifact: chat is ephemeral and the user is reading THIS message, so restating a verify command from two turns ago is not duplication and must not be cut. Written as "already sent", with prior replies fed in as context, it deleted the table, the code block and the verify command together in 2 of 8 live runs, leaving one sentence. Prior chat replies are therefore not a deduplication source. Nothing here competes with the invariants; the objective was simply written wrong.

fields.title: Agent-invoked session machinery defaults to --db main; only human-typed commands must name the database
fields.description: Carve-out from ED-1561, which requires an agent to name --db on every command reaching a database in a self_dev project. That is right for commands an agent CHOOSES to run against project data, and wrong for machinery it runs mechanically every turn under a contract: there the correct database is not the caller判 judgement, it is fixed by whatever reads the result. endless task report is the instance -- the Stop hook that consumes its checkpoint pins main unconditionally, so any other routing puts writer and reader on different databases and the gate blocks every turn as "never reported". Such a surface defaults to main when given no --db, as hook/channel/tmux already do; an explicit --db still wins. The test is not "does an agent type it" but "does something else already fix which database is correct".

payload.title: Stop sandbox-routed decision add and update from committing a doc mirror onto the worktree branch
payload.description: A sandbox-routed `endless --db sandbox decision add` writes a decision mirror file into the WORKTREE under .endless/decisions and auto-commits it on the task branch ("Endless: add decision ED-1"). Hit twice while smoke-testing E-1920; both commits had to be reset away by hand, and a session that did not check `git log` would have landed sandbox test fixtures into main. DB writes route to the sandbox correctly, but the E-1747 doc-mirror half of the same command does not: it resolves a project root and commits there regardless of which DB the write went to. Sandbox decision IDs also start at 1, colliding with the real ledger's ED-1 and ED-2.

triage.rationale: it's unclear whether the fix should suppress the doc-mirror commit entirely when sandbox-routed, redirect it into the sandbox, or namespace sandbox decision IDs to avoid collision with the real ledger, and the description doesn't pick one.

payload.title: Stop reporting a missing column as an uninitialized database
payload.description: A query that fails because a column is missing is reported as `endless database is uninitialized ... db file: exists but has no endless schema`, which sends the reader to the wrong problem entirely. Hit on E-1920: `decision show` selected a column added by an unapplied schema change, and the message claimed the whole DB was uninitialized while `decision list` (not selecting that column) worked fine in the same second. The handler should distinguish a missing-table or missing-column error from a genuinely unschema'd file, and name the column and the change file to apply.

triage.rationale: The description names the exact bug, root cause, and required fix shape (distinguish missing-table/column errors from uninitialized-DB errors, and name the column and change file in the message).

fields.title: Route every file a sandbox-mode command writes to the sandbox, not just the DB and ledger
fields.description: `--db sandbox` isolates the DB and, since E-1729, the event ledger — but nothing else. Every other file a command writes still resolves a REAL project root and git-commits there. Hit on E-1920: a sandbox-routed `decision add` wrote decision mirrors into the worktree and auto-committed two junk commits onto the task branch. E-1729 already fixed this exact mechanism for the ledger and established the shape (sandbox-local dir under ConfigDir, no git commit, since a sandbox is disposable and not a repo), but it was applied at one call site instead of made a rule, so E-1747's doc mirrors re-broke it. Make the DB target govern every artifact write, so the next mirror-writing feature cannot reintroduce it.

triage.rationale: it doesn't specify the mechanism for making the DB target "govern every artifact write" (e.g., a shared routing abstraction/interface all write call sites must go through) or which call sites beyond decision/doc mirrors are in scope.

payload.title: Stop calling the SQLite database the ledger
payload.description: The db-ledger is Endless's permanent record and the SQLite database is a rebuildable projection of it, so using 'ledger' for the database conflates the two — including in the user-facing --db refusal text an agent reads when it gets the flag wrong. 31 sites in live code, docs and templates; the 80 in tests/tasks/*-verify.sh are deliberately out of scope, being spent pre-land gates.
payload.analysis:
# "Ledger" already means something else

The db-ledger (`.endless/db-ledger/*.jsonl`) is the permanent record of task
state; the SQLite database is a rebuildable projection of it. CLAUDE.md says so
in its own words. Using "ledger" for the database collapses the distinction that
architecture rests on, and it does it in the two places most likely to mislead:
agent-facing comments, and the user-facing `--db` refusal.

## Scope

31 sites in live code, docs and templates. Two are user-facing:

    src/endless/config.py:328   "  --db main     the real ledger — managing the project"
    src/endless/cli.py:302      "--db main (the real ledger) or --db sandbox (this worktree's test DB). "

The rest are comments, docstrings and two guide pages. `internal/monitor/db.go`
carries the most, and is where the term does the most damage — it is the file
that decides which database a process opens.

## Explicitly OUT of scope: `tests/tasks/*-verify.sh`

There are 80 more occurrences there. Leave every one of them.

A verify script is a pre-land gate, valid only immediately before its own land,
in its own worktree. A landed one is spent — nothing should ever run it again —
so its wording cannot mislead anyone and editing it is churn against an artifact
with no future. E-1975 already filed and declined a task (E-2033) that misread
this rule; do not re-derive it.

## Wording

`--db main` and `--db sandbox` already establish the vocabulary. Say "the main
database" and "the sandbox database" (or "this worktree's sandbox"). Avoid "real
ledger", "the real DB" and "the ledger" wherever the SQLite database is meant.

The user-facing strings deserve Mike's eye rather than a mechanical
substitution: the refusal text is the first thing an agent hits when it gets the
flag wrong, and it is currently the clearest statement in the product of what
the two databases are for.

triage.rationale: the description doesn't state what terminology should replace "ledger" for the database (e.g., naming for the SQLite projection, the --db refusal text, and other 31 sites) or how to distinguish it consistently from the real ledger.

payload.title: Stop auto-registering a worktree as its own project when the project walk-up misses
payload.description: Five worktrees are registered as top-level projects (names e-1944, e-1914, e-1975, e-1920, e-1733), so the walk-up in ProjectIDForPath and _project_root_for_cwd stops AT the worktree. Consequence: `esp` in a worktree resolves the worktree as its own project root and is a no-op, stranding the user. Written by monitor.ensureAutoRegisteredProject, which names by directory basename and INSERTs straight into the DB with no project.registered event, so the rows are invisible in the ledger and would vanish on rebuild-db. All five appeared only after E-2011 landed, and all five store an ABSOLUTE path while every legitimate row is home-relative, so the writer did not apply E-2011's storage form — a stale worktree-local endless-go misses at every rung of the walk and falls through to auto-register. The durable fix is a guard: auto-registration must never fire for a directory under .endless/worktrees — a worktree always belongs to its parent project.

triage.rationale: The description pins down the exact bug (worktree-under-.endless auto-registers as its own project via ensureAutoRegisteredProject), diagnoses the root cause (walk-up miss due to stale storage-form mismatch from E-2011), and states the fix precisely (guard auto-registration against paths under .endless/worktrees).

fields.title: Refuse to run a worktree binary against a main DB whose schema it cannot read
fields.description: The e-2011-home-relative-project-paths change file was applied to the shared main DB at 2026-08-20T18:17:55, converting projects.path from absolute to home-relative. In self-dev, every worktree carries its OWN bin/endless-go built at its branch point, and 114 of 156 worktrees hold a binary built before that moment. Those binaries compare a raw absolute cwd against a column that now holds ~/..., miss every rung of ProjectIDForPath's walk-up, and fall through to ensureAutoRegisteredProject — which silently registers the worktree as a project named after its directory. Zero stray rows exist before 18:17:55 and every one after it. Nothing checks that a binary can READ the database it opens: _schema_version already names every applied change, so a binary opening a DB carrying a marker it does not ship should refuse loudly instead of misreading. E-2011 is not the bug; it is the first format change to expose a standing hazard that every future one repeats.

payload.title: Stop the minimizer deleting direct answers to questions the user explicitly asked
payload.description: The user asked two explicit questions — "won't they just re-register until we fix it?" and "why did it start happening?" — and the minimizer deleted the answer to both, keeping only a side concern the user had raised in passing. The appeal pass, whose whole purpose is restoring an over-aggressive cut, deleted MORE: it dropped the appeal argument itself plus the remaining framing, leaving four disconnected fragments. Net effect: the user asked why a bug started, the session determined the cause with timestamp evidence, and the user received none of it. The failure mode looks like the minimizer scoring inline evidence blocks and causal narrative as unrequested elaboration, while scoring short factual bullets as responsive — exactly inverted when the request was itself a why-question. Worth adding to the corpus as a case where the denylist must not fire: content that directly answers an interrogative in the user's message.

triage.rationale: it names a failure mode and a corpus goal but leaves open how the minimizer/denylist should detect "content answering an interrogative" and how that rule integrates with existing scoring.

the description names the hazard but leaves open how a binary should detect and enforce version compatibility (e.g., minimum required change list, error vs. refuse-and-exit behavior, where the check lives, and how it interacts with auto-migration).

payload.title: Add a 0-based offset to task report --raw so earlier drafts are reachable
payload.description: `task report --raw` is a bare boolean flag (is_flag=True) that prints only the newest draft, so there is no way to reach an earlier one. The storage already supports it fully: session_gates keeps one relay row per turn with raw_draft, and session_gates_corpus indexes exactly those rows newest-first for scanning. Only the CLI surface is missing. Wanted: an optional 0-based offset, where --raw is the newest, --raw 1 the one before it, --raw 2 the one before that. Click supports this on the existing flag via flag_value so the bare form keeps working. Two details worth settling: an appeal turn writes a second row, so offsets count DRAFTS not turns and an appealed turn consumes two; and an offset past the end should say how many drafts exist rather than print nothing.

triage.rationale: The description names the exact mechanism (Click flag_value on the existing flag), the semantics (0-based, newest-first, counting drafts not turns), and the required error behavior for out-of-range offsets, leaving no material design decision unresolved.

fields.description: `task report --raw` is a bare boolean flag printing only the newest draft; earlier ones are unreachable from the CLI though session_gates retains every one, indexed newest-first. PRIOR ART: E-1959's analysis already designed the read surface — `report log` listing triples (id, prompt excerpt, raw/minimized sizes, label) and `report show <id>` rendering raw and minimized side by side, with the command shape settled as a restructure rather than a sibling group. Those decisions lapsed when E-1975 replaced E-1959; this task revives the minimum of them. Prefer list-then-show-by-id over an offset: an id is unambiguous, and it sidesteps the counting problem. If an offset is kept it MUST count TURNS, not drafts — an appeal writes a second row, and drafts are invisible to the user, who can only count the replies they saw.

fields.title: Restore a read surface for earlier minimizer drafts (report log / report show)
Make an appeal actually able to restore an over-cut draft, not just re-minimize it
fields.description: An appeal is sold to the agent as the recourse for an over-aggressive cut, but nothing implements that. report_cmd runs the appeal through the SAME minimize prompt with no separate prompt and no relationship to the pass it appeals, so it is simply another independent minimization whose input happens to contain an argument — free to return LESS than what it is appealing. Observed twice in one session on E-1920: the first pass dropped the answers to two directly-asked questions, and the appeal dropped those plus the appeal argument itself, leaving disconnected fragments; the agent then had no recourse left because the budget is one. No prompt wording can fix this, which is why it is a task rather than a denylist override — monotonicity is a mechanical property, like the invariant vetoes. Options: require the appeal's output to cover the spans it argues for, or present both passes and let the user pick.

triage.rationale: the description names two mutually exclusive options (enforce span-coverage vs. present both passes for user choice) without choosing between them, leaving the actual implementation mechanism undecided.

The description fully specifies the command shape (`report log` listing id/prompt excerpt/sizes/label, `report show <id>` rendering raw vs minimized) and the id-vs-offset tradeoff with a clear counting rule, leaving no material design decision open.

payload.title: Honor a hand-edited minimize instruction instead of ignoring it
payload.description: endless task report reads the instruction it shortens replies with from the minimizer_champions table, and never from the minimize line in .endless/report-prompts.jsonl. So a hand-written instruction has had no effect since the first time the background job promoted one, and nothing says so — while denylist, judge and generate overrides in the same file still work. report_prompts.py's own docstring promises the opposite.
payload.analysis:
# Terms, before anything else

**The instruction.** When `endless task report` shortens an agent's reply, it
calls a model and hands it two things: the agent's full draft, and a block of
text telling the model what to cut. That block is the instruction.

**The overrides file.** `.endless/report-prompts.jsonl` holds one JSON object
per line, each with a `name` and a `text`. The line whose `name` is `"minimize"`
supplies a hand-written instruction. There are three other recognised names —
`denylist`, `judge`, `generate`.

**The two tables.** `minimizer_variants` stores instructions, each keyed by a
hash of its own text. `minimizer_champions` holds the hash of the one in use.

**The background job.** `minimizer-loop`. Every ten minutes it scores shortenings
that already happened. Less often it asks a model to write a new instruction,
tries it against the one in use over drafts already stored, and rewrites
`minimizer_champions` to point at the new one if it did better.

# The defect

`endless task report` reads the instruction from `minimizer_champions`. It never
reads the `minimize` line. So a hand-written instruction has no effect from the
first promotion onward, and nothing says so.

The other three names still work: `denylist`, `judge` and `generate` are read
from the file on every call.

Demonstrated:

    override text present in what the model gets: False
    denylist override path still splices: True

`src/endless/report_prompts.py` states the opposite in its own docstring —
"Editing an OVERRIDE needs no task and no land. That is the whole point of the
layer." That sentence is true for three of the four names and false for the one
that matters.

A hand-edited instruction does take effect after `endless minimizer reseed`,
which rebuilds the champion from the shipped defaults plus the overrides file.
Nothing points that out, and it is a strange thing to have to know.

# Why the fix is not one line

Every shortening Endless stores also stores, in `session_gates.variant_hash`,
the hash of the instruction that produced it. If `task report` used the
hand-written instruction but still wrote the champion's hash there, that column
would name an instruction which did not produce that reply.

The background job reads those rows to decide whether the instruction in use is
any good. It would be scoring the champion using replies the hand-written
instruction produced — and promoting or rejecting on that basis. Fixing the
visible problem would quietly corrupt the evidence the job learns from.

# Proposed fix

When the overrides file has a `minimize` line:

  1. insert that text into `minimizer_variants`, which gives it its own hash;
  2. use it for the shortening;
  3. write THAT hash into `session_gates.variant_hash`.

It does not become the champion. `minimizer_champions` keeps pointing where it
pointed, so removing the line returns to the job's instruction with nothing lost.

# Open question for Mike

While a hand-written instruction is in force, should the background job keep
promoting new ones underneath it? Promotions would be invisible in the replies
and would take effect the moment the line is deleted. Stopping the job instead
means an override silently freezes learning. Either is defensible; the choice
should be explicit, and `endless minimizer status` should say which is happening.

triage.rationale: The bug and its fix are fully specified — read the minimize instruction from report-prompts.jsonl the same way denylist/judge/generate overrides already do, matching the docstring's promised behavior.

fields.title: Add report log and report show commands for reading past drafts
fields.description: There is no way to read a past draft. `task report --raw` prints only the newest one, so once a reply is minimized the user cannot see what was cut, and cannot judge or label it. Add `report log` to list recent drafts and `report show <id>` to display one with its raw and minimized text side by side. Design already settled in ED-1959; see the link.

There is no way to read a past draft. `task report --raw` prints only the newest one, so once a reply is minimized the user cannot see what was cut, and cannot judge or label it. Add `report log` to list recent drafts and `report show <id>` to display one with its raw and minimized text side by side. Design already settled in E-1959; see the link.

triage.rationale: The commands, their arguments, and output shape (list of drafts; raw and minimized side by side) are specified, with design already settled in the referenced task E-1959.

payload.title: Make the reply minimizer trustworthy enough to leave enabled
payload.description: The reply minimizer ships enabled but has never been calibrated: no way to read what it cut, no working recourse when it cuts wrongly, and a self-tuning loop that has never run. Disabled in this project until the pieces that make it safe to leave on exist. Holds that work.

triage.rationale: the description names goals (auditability, recourse, working self-tuning) but not the mechanisms or interfaces for any of them, leaving materially different designs open.

payload.title: Add an observe-only minimizer mode that records drafts without cutting or enforcing
payload.description: Turning the minimizer off also stops drafts being recorded, so the corpus stops growing during exactly the period it would be most useful to accumulate one. Add a third state between on and off: the agent still writes its draft through `task report`, the draft and the turn's context are still recorded, but nothing is cut and nothing is enforced — the agent sends its own reply. That keeps a replayable corpus building while the channel is untrusted, so when it is switched back on there is real material to calibrate against instead of starting from zero.

triage.rationale: leaves open how the existing on/off state is represented and where the third "observe" state plugs into the current enable check, config schema, and command flow.

fields.text:
# E-2035 — the DB target must govern file writes, not just the DB

## Problem

`--db sandbox` isolates the database and, since E-1729, the event ledger. It
governs nothing else. Every other file a command writes still resolves a REAL
project root and git-commits there.

Concrete: a sandbox-routed `endless --db sandbox decision add` wrote decision
mirrors into a worktree and auto-committed two junk commits ("Endless: add
decision ED-1", "ED-2") onto a task branch. They had to be reset by hand; a
session that did not check `git log` would have landed sandbox fixtures into
main. Sandbox ids start at 1, so the files also collide with the real ledger's
ED-1 / ED-2 namespace.

E-1729 already fixed this exact mechanism for the ledger and established the
shape — sandbox-local directory under the sandbox config dir, and NO git commit,
because a sandbox is disposable and is not a repo. That fix was applied at one
call site instead of made a rule, so E-1747's doc mirrors reintroduced it.

## Approach

Make "where do artifacts go" a function of the resolved DB target, in one place,
rather than a decision each writer makes independently.

1. **One resolver.** A single accessor answering "artifact root for the current
   target" — the project root under `--db main`, the sandbox config dir under
   `--db sandbox` — plus "may I commit?" (false in sandbox, always). Python
   side has `config.RESOLVED_CONFIG_DIR` already pinned by `apply_db_choice`,
   so the target is known; nothing consults it for file paths today.

2. **Route every writer through it.** Known writers:
   - `decision_cmd._mirror_decision_body` / `_commit_doc_on_main`
   - `task_cmd._mirror_doc_to_worktree` (plans, outcomes, analysis) and
     `worktree_cmd._commit_doc_in_worktree`
   - `worktree_cmd._materialize_task_docs`
   Audit for others rather than trusting this list.

3. **Suppress, do not relocate, where the artifact has no meaning.** A decision
   mirror exists to give a REAL decision version-controlled history. A sandbox
   decision has no history worth keeping, so the mirror should not be written at
   all — cheaper and less surprising than writing files into a cache dir nobody
   reads. Same reasoning for task doc mirrors.

4. **Make the rule enforceable.** A test that runs the mirror-writing commands
   under `--db sandbox` and asserts the git status of both the worktree and the
   main checkout is unchanged. Without it the next artifact-writing feature
   reintroduces this a third time, which is the actual failure mode here.

## Verification

- `--db sandbox decision add` writes no file under any git checkout and creates
  no commit; the DB row still lands in the sandbox.
- Same for `task update --text` / `--outcome` / `--analysis` under sandbox.
- Under `--db main` every mirror is written and committed exactly as today.
- The regression test above fails if a writer is added that bypasses the
  resolver.

## Note on scope

This is deliberately the rule, not the decision-mirror bug. Filing the single
call site is what let it recur after E-1729.

# E-2038 — refuse a binary that cannot read the DB it opens

## Problem

The `e-2011-home-relative-project-paths` change file ran against the shared main
DB at 2026-08-20T18:17:55, rewriting `projects.path` from absolute to `~/...`.
In self-dev every worktree carries its own `bin/endless-go`, built at its branch
point, so the migration instantly created a fleet of readers that cannot read
the new format. They compare a raw absolute cwd against a `~/...` column, miss
every rung of `ProjectIDForPath`'s walk-up, and fall through to
`ensureAutoRegisteredProject`, which silently registers the worktree as a
project named after its directory.

Evidence: zero stray project rows before that timestamp, five after. All five
store an ABSOLUTE path while every legitimate row is home-relative — proof the
writer predates E-2011. `e-1914` and `e-1733` run Aug-13 binaries with no
`homeRelative` symbol at all. At the time of measurement 114 of 156 worktrees
held a binary older than the migration.

E-2011 is not the bug. It is the first format change to expose a standing
hazard: nothing checks that a binary can read the database it opens, so every
future migration repeats this.

## Approach

`_schema_version` already names every applied change file, and a binary ships a
known set under `internal/schema/changes/`. That is the handshake.

1. **Compare at open.** In `monitor.DB()`, after schema application, read
   `_schema_version` and compare against the embedded change-file set. Markers
   in the DB that the binary does not ship mean the DB is AHEAD of the binary.

2. **Refuse loudly, and name both sides.** Exit non-zero with the unknown
   marker(s) and the remedy (`just build` in this worktree, or run main's
   binary). Silent misreading is the failure being fixed; a quiet degrade
   repeats it.

3. **Ahead-only, never behind.** A binary shipping changes the DB has not
   applied is normal — that is every pre-land worktree, and `apply-change` is
   how it resolves. Only DB-ahead-of-binary is refused.

4. **Do not gate the escape hatches.** `db apply-change`, `db path`, `db backup`
   and `rebuild-db` must still run, or a refused binary cannot be recovered
   with the tools that exist to recover it.

## Interaction with E-1704

E-1704 makes one binary self-re-exec into the worktree build. That does not
remove this: re-exec still lands in the stale build. The version check belongs
IN the routing decision — "re-exec only into a build that can read this DB,
else stay in main's" — which turns a hard refusal into a graceful fallback.
Sequence this after E-1704 if that lands first; the check is the same code.

## Cleanup (separate from the guard)

Five stray rows exist. Removing them is `project unregister <name>`, ONE name
per invocation. Note `tasks`, `decisions`, `notes`, `activity` and
`project_next` are `ON DELETE CASCADE` from `projects`; measured at filing time
these rows held 0 tasks, 0 decisions, 0 sessions and 153 activity rows. Cleanup
without the guard is temporary — any stale worktree re-registers on its next
hook event.

## Verification

- A DB carrying a `_schema_version` marker absent from the binary's change set
  is refused, and the message names the marker.
- A binary with changes the DB lacks runs normally.
- `db apply-change` / `db path` / `db backup` / `rebuild-db` run against an
  ahead DB.
- With the guard in place, a deliberately stale binary run from a worktree
  registers no project row.

# E-2039 — make an appeal able to restore an over-cut draft

## Problem

The appeal is presented to the agent as the recourse for an over-aggressive cut
("--raw prints it back unchanged, which is what makes an over-aggressive cut
recoverable"), but nothing implements restoration. `report_cmd` runs the appeal
through the SAME minimize prompt, with no separate prompt and no reference to
the pass being appealed. It is simply a second, independent minimization whose
input happens to contain an argument — free to return LESS.

Observed twice in one session: pass 1 deleted the answers to two directly-asked
questions; the appeal deleted those AND the appeal argument itself, leaving
disconnected fragments. Budget is one, so there was no third try.

## Why this is not a prompt fix

Monotonicity is a property of the RELATIONSHIP between two outputs. A prompt can
ask for it and cannot guarantee it, and the optimizer can only tune wording. The
existing invariant vetoes are in Python for exactly this reason.

## Approach

Give the appeal a different job from the first pass. It is not "minimize again";
it is "reinstate specific material into an existing minimization."

1. **The appeal sees the first pass.** Build a distinct `appeal` prompt entry
   (new key in `report_prompts.DEFAULTS`, so it is overridable like the others)
   taking the raw draft, the FIRST pass's output, and the agent's argument. Its
   instruction is to return the first output plus the material the argument
   justifies — not to re-edit from scratch.

2. **Mechanical floor.** After the appeal returns, verify it is a superset of
   the first pass on protected content (`minimizer_invariants.has_protected_
   content` already identifies code blocks, tables, commands). If the appeal
   dropped protected content the first pass kept, reject the appeal and keep
   pass 1 — a failed appeal must never be worse than not appealing.

3. **Length floor.** Reject an appeal output shorter than the pass it appeals.
   Blunt, but the appeal's whole premise is that something was missing; a
   shorter result is definitionally not that. Cheap, no model call, no judgment.

4. **On rejection, say so.** Print pass 1 with a one-line note that the appeal
   was refused and why. Silence here would read as "the appeal ran and this is
   its output", which is the confusion that makes the current behavior invisible.

## Corpus

An appeal already writes its own row. Record which row it appeals (`appeals_
gate_id`, nullable) so the pair is queryable — today an appeal is
indistinguishable from an ordinary turn, which is also why offsets into draft
history are ambiguous (see E-2040).

## Verification

- An appeal that argues for a cut paragraph returns pass 1 PLUS that paragraph.
- An appeal whose output drops a code block or command present in pass 1 is
  rejected, and pass 1 is printed instead.
- An appeal shorter than pass 1 is rejected.
- A rejected appeal still consumes the budget (it ran) and says it was rejected.
- The appeal row records the gate it appeals.

## Open question

Whether a rejected appeal should refund the budget. Argument for: the agent got
nothing. Against: it spent a model call, and refunding invites retry-until-lucky
— the exact behavior the one-appeal bound exists to prevent. Default to no
refund unless the user prefers otherwise.

# E-2043 — observe-only minimizer mode

## Problem

`minimizer.enabled` is boolean. Off means the whole report channel is off: the
agent is not told to use `task report`, the Stop hook does not enforce it, and
no draft is recorded. So switching the minimizer off to stop it damaging replies
also stops the corpus growing — during exactly the period when accumulating one
is most valuable, because that corpus is what a later re-enable would be
calibrated against.

## Approach

Add a third state to the existing switch rather than a fourth config key.
`project_minimizer_config` (`src/endless/config.py`) already normalizes three
spellings into `{enabled, optimizer}`; add `"minimizer": {"mode": "observe"}`
alongside the booleans, normalizing to a third field rather than overloading
`enabled` — a boolean that has three meanings is how the E-1953/E-1975 rename
confusion started.

Resolved shape: `{"enabled": bool, "optimizer": bool, "observe": bool}`.
`observe` is meaningful only when `enabled` is false; when both are false the
channel is fully off, as today.

In observe mode:

- The agent IS instructed to run `task report --draft-file` (guide + handoff
  text keyed off the same config read that already omits them when off).
- `report_cmd` records the corpus row — `user_prompt`, `raw_draft`,
  `fetched_context`, `variant_hash`, `task_type` — and runs the fetch policy,
  since replay needs the context record.
- It does NOT call the minimizer. No model call, no `sanctioned_text`.
- It echoes the draft back unchanged, so the agent's own reply is what ships.
- The Stop hook does not compare the final message to anything.

`sanctioned_text` NULL is the marker for "recorded, never minimized". Corpus
selection in `minimizer_store` already requires `sanctioned_text IS NOT NULL`,
so observe rows are excluded from replay automatically — no filter change, and
they still serve as (prompt, draft, context) triples a future champion can be
replayed against once one exists.

## Go mirror

`monitor.readMinimizer` must learn the same third state or the Go hook and the
Python CLI will disagree about whether to enforce. Same closed set of spellings.

## Verification

- Config with `{"mode": "observe"}` resolves to `enabled=false, observe=true` in
  both Python and Go, and the two agree on every spelling in the existing table.
- A report in observe mode writes a `session_gates` row with `raw_draft` and
  `fetched_context` set and `sanctioned_text` NULL, makes no model call, and
  prints the draft byte-for-byte.
- The Stop hook accepts a final message that differs from anything.
- `minimizer_store.corpus(...)` does not return observe rows.
- Fully-off remains fully off: no instruction, no row, no enforcement.

## Open question

Whether observe mode should still run the JUDGE (which scores fidelity of a
minimization) — it cannot, since there is no minimization to score. So observe
rows carry no judgment and `evidence()` sees nothing from them. That is correct
but worth stating: observe builds replay material, not supervision signal. Only
labels and A/B picks supply supervision, and both need the channel on.

payload.title: Remove the report-prompts.jsonl override layer
payload.description: An optional overrides file from E-1771 that nobody can use and that does not work. Its main entry, minimize, is the entire 5307-character instruction on one escaped JSON line, and per E-2041 task report never reads it anyway. Mike cut the CLAUDE.md pointer to it on 2026-08-20 and named it directly on 2026-08-22. The premise — tuning wording without a task and a land — is now served by the loop and by endless minimizer reseed.
payload.analysis:
# What the file is

`.endless/report-prompts.jsonl` is an optional overrides file introduced by
E-1771 (commit 23d35ffb) and modelled on `verbs.jsonl` (E-1268). It is read from
two places, project first:

    <project>/.endless/report-prompts.jsonl
    ~/.config/endless/report-prompts.jsonl

Nothing creates it. Neither exists on Mike's machine, and the instruction in use
is the one embedded in `src/endless/report_prompts.py`.

It recognises four names: `minimize`, `denylist`, `judge`, `generate`.

# Why it should go

**Nobody can use it for the thing it exists for.** `minimize` is the whole
instruction, not a tweak: 5307 characters over 75 lines, which must contain
`{prompt}`, `{context}`, `{draft}` and `{denylist}`. As one JSON line that is a
5458-character string with every newline escaped. It has never been written.

**And it would not work if it were.** Per E-2041, `task report` reads the
instruction from `minimizer_champions` and never consults this file, so a
`minimize` line has had no effect since the loop first promoted anything.

**Mike has objected to it twice.** On 2026-08-20 (session 7ffe2a27) he cut the
CLAUDE.md line that pointed at it. On 2026-08-22 (session 2a04f666) he named it
directly: "I nixed that."

**The premise it was built on is gone.** The layer existed so wording could be
tuned without a task and a land. E-1975 replaced that with a loop that tunes the
wording automatically, and `endless minimizer reseed` for taking a shipped fix.
The remaining need — pinning a hand-written instruction — is E-2041's subject and
does not need a JSONL file to satisfy.

# Scope

Remove the file's resolution entirely: `_read_layer`, `_machine_path`,
`_project_path` and `load_prompts`'s layering in `src/endless/report_prompts.py`,
plus the tests that cover them and any doc that mentions the file.

`denylist`, `judge` and `generate` currently resolve through the same layer and
do work. Decide per name whether anything is lost by fixing them to the embedded
default. `denylist` is the one with a plausible claim, since ED-1557's design
anticipated appending an offending phrase to it.

# Consequence for E-2041

E-2041 asks that a hand-written `minimize` line be honoured. If this file is
removed, that task is answered by removal rather than by implementation, and
should be superseded rather than worked.

triage.rationale: The description names the exact file to remove, cites why it's dead code (unread since E-2041, unreachable since the CLAUDE.md pointer was cut), and states the replacement mechanism, leaving only a mechanical deletion.

fields.analysis:
# Evidence: the shipped label channel dropped 90% of what the user sent

Measured 2026-08-16 over `session_messages` since E-1953 landed, counting
line-leading `$TOKEN` uses in user messages:

| sigil          |  n | status                        |
|----------------|----|-------------------------------|
| `$PUFFERY`     |  8 | not in vocabulary — ignored   |
| `$DUPLICATION` |  6 | ignored                       |
| `$JARGON`      |  3 | ignored                       |
| `$UNCLEAR`     |  3 | ignored                       |
| `$UNNECESSARY` |  3 | ignored                       |
| `$FORMATTING`  |  2 | ignored                       |
| `$NOTE`        |  1 | ignored                       |
| `$DEFY`        |  1 | ignored                       |
| `$MISSING`     |  1 | ignored                       |
| `$CUT`         |  1 | recognised                    |
| `$GOOD`        |  1 | recognised                    |
| `$WRONG`       |  1 | recognised                    |

**31 uses, 3 recognised.** `session_gates` holds exactly one label row, attached
to a pre-E-1953 relay checkpoint with no `raw_draft` — i.e. not even a corpus
sample. The mechanism was never disabled and never failed to fire; it fired
every time and rejected silently, because `scanSigils` matches only
`CUT|BLOAT|WRONG|GOOD|FULL` and an unrecognised token produces no match, no
record, and no error. The one "not recorded" notice that does exist covers only
a BARE known label, so it never fired either.

Two things follow, and they are different tasks.

## 1. The vocabulary was the wrong ontology (owned by ED-1555 / E-1975)

E-1953 shipped labels about the MINIMIZER'S PERFORMANCE — did it cut too much
(`$CUT`) or too little (`$BLOAT`). The user types labels about the REPLY'S
DEFECTS — puffery, duplication, jargon, formatting, unclear. Only `$WRONG`
overlaps. The user was never grading the minimizer; they were critiquing the
writing.

This is empirical support for ED-1555 (free-form, discovered from use), which is
still `proposed`. Recorded here rather than edited into that decision because
E-1975 is underway in another session.

Note the immediate consequence for E-1975 — and note that it does NOT require
the user to type a token. A classifier reading "this is puffery" or "seam is
jargon" recognises the shape as well as `$PUFFERY` would. What matters is that
critiques of this shape ARE denylist entries. The minimize prompt already carries an anti-puffery section with phrase
anchors, so a critique of that shape can append straight to
`report-prompts.jsonl` — config, no task, no land, no batch job, no judge. That
is a real consumer of user feedback available today, and it is upstream of the
whole optimizer loop.

## 2. The CHANNEL is in-band, and that is this task

ED-1555 fixes the mechanism as `$TOKEN "quoted span"` typed into a prompt.
Everything typed into a prompt is visible to the agent by construction, so the
agent responds to the critique. The user's stated complaint is that this
commentary is itself the thing being criticised, and that it persists after
being told to stop — which is the same failure that motivated the minimizer.

Channels ranked by whether silence is structural:

- **Sibling terminal pane** — `endless feedback ...` run in another pane.
  Claude never sees it. The ONLY structurally silent option.
- **`!cmd` in the prompt** — NOT silent. Tested 2026-08-16: `! echo ''`
  produced "No output, as expected. Ready when you are."
- **Slash-command skill** — not silent. "Run this and say nothing" is a
  guideline; a skill body cannot bind the model's final message.
- **In-band `$TOKEN`** — the current design; least silent of all.

## Build shape

- `endless feedback` CLI, **prose critique only — no vocabulary at all**, not
  even an optional one. The requester's position (2026-08-16) is explicit: they
  do not want to reach for `$PUFFERY` when they can write "this is puffery", or
  `$JARGON` when they can write "seam is jargon, explain what you mean, don't
  use seam". A token the user has to recall is the same tax whether it is
  required or optional. The ONLY structured element in the whole surface is the
  optional span reference.
- Optional span reference. The user's preferred notation is `P<n>` for a
  paragraph of the last reply and `T<n>:P<n>` to reach back a turn, chosen over
  `$<n>` specifically to avoid shell escaping. The user is content to count
  paragraphs by eye; a `--show` that prints the numbered reply from
  `session_messages` is a convenience, not a requirement.
- Repeatable, so several critiques land in one invocation:
  `endless feedback P1 '...' T2:P3 '...'`
- **Silent on success. Loud on every rejection.** This is the rule the evidence
  above bought: an unparseable reference, an unknown flag, a missing session —
  each must fail visibly. 28 dropped signals is what silent rejection costs.
- A `/e-feedback` skill as the front door for users who will not open a
  terminal, accepting that it comments. Adoption argument, not a functional one:
  skills are the culturally legible surface, and a better CLI with no on-ramp
  loses to a worse skill with one. Skill body stays a thin template over the
  CLI so the binary owns parsing and validation (see
  docs/private/research-2026-08-15-skills-arguments.md, option 3).

## Open

- Whether the agent may ever call `endless feedback` itself. If it may, the
  CLI can print "Reply ONLY with 'Ok'" — still a guideline, but positioned in a
  tool result immediately before composition, and the worst case is one word of
  noise rather than a whole reply. Low stakes make a guideline acceptable here
  in a way it was not for the minimizer.
- Whether out-of-band invocation can resolve WHICH session the feedback is
  about. A sibling pane has no session id of its own; it needs the tmux window's
  session, which `endless` already resolves elsewhere (E-1585).



---

## Update, 2026-08-22 (ES-1104, while landing E-1975)

**ED-1555 was rejected.** The in-band `$TOKEN "quoted span"` mechanism this task
replaces no longer has a decision behind it.

**E-1975 shipped that mechanism anyway, and widened it.**
`internal/hookcmd/sigils.go` now accepts any uppercase token, not only
`CUT|BLOAT|WRONG|GOOD|FULL`, and records one row per quoted span. That fixed the
defect measured on 2026-08-16 — 31 uses, 3 recognised, `$PUFFERY` (8),
`$DUPLICATION` (6), `$JARGON` (3) and the rest silently ignored — but it did not
retire the channel. It made the rejected channel work better.

**So retiring it now belongs here**, or in a task filed against this one:
`scanSigils`, its `applySigils` / `stageReportTurn` hook wiring, the
`report_labels` table's write path, and the `$A`/`$B`/`$MORE`/`$LESS` directives
that ride the same parse. Otherwise a rejected mechanism ships indefinitely
alongside the replacement this task builds.

Note the directives are NOT all feedback: `$A`/`$B` pick between two offered
minimizations and `$FULL` licenses one un-minimized reply. Those are commands to
Endless, not critique, so decide per sigil whether `endless feedback` absorbs it
or it needs its own home before deleting the parse.

payload.title: Feedback on a reply is out-of-band; nothing replaces the sigils in band
payload.description: Three steps, ending where it started: a fixed set (CUT/BLOAT/WRONG/GOOD), then any freeform token, then none. A sigil the user types sits in the prompt, so the agent sees it and comments on it — at length, which is exactly what the minimizer exists to stop. Measured on 2026-08-16: 31 uses, 3 recognised, and the ones that worked invited a reply about the criticism. So critique moves out of band to an endless feedback command, run in a pane the agent never sees, silent on success and loud on rejection. Nothing takes the sigils' place in band: a model can read sentiment from the user's ordinary words, so a special syntax buys nothing while costing a vocabulary nobody can recall mid-complaint. Reverses ED-1555.
